question: Why must a Custom Element name contain a hyphen?

options.text: It is a developer style convention
options.explanation: No, this is a W3C specification requirement, not just a convention.

options.text: To prevent conflicts with future native HTML elements in the browser
options.explanation: The specification requires a hyphen so that the namespace of names like 'my-element' never collides with standard HTML elements such as 'div', 'section', or 'dialog'.
Parsing performance does not depend on whether a tag name contains a hyphen.

options.text: To distinguish Web Components from element attributes
options.explanation: Attributes and tags have different syntax in HTML — a hyphen is not needed to tell them apart.

question: Which CustomEvent parameter allows an event to cross the Shadow DOM boundary and bubble up to the document?

options.explanation: bubbles: true allows an event to bubble up the DOM tree, but it stops at the Shadow DOM boundary.
composed: true is the key parameter for crossing the shadow boundary. Without it, events stay inside the Shadow DOM even when bubbles: true is set.
cancelable affects whether the event can be cancelled via preventDefault(), but has no effect on crossing the shadow boundary.
detail is simply the event payload; it does not affect event routing.

question: Which of the following does NOT penetrate the Shadow DOM boundary?

options.explanation: CSS Custom Properties intentionally cross the shadow boundary — this is the primary mechanism for customizing Web Components.

Regular CSS rules do not penetrate into the Shadow DOM — that is the whole point of style encapsulation. Styles inside the component do not 'leak' out, and styles outside do not affect the component's internals.
Inherited CSS properties (font-family, font-size, color) are inherited into the Shadow DOM — this allows typography to be set at the application level.
JS properties are directly accessible on the DOM element — the shadow boundary does not affect their availability.

question: You are building a Web Component for a micro-frontend architecture. You need to pass an array of product objects into the component. What is the correct way to do this?

options.explanation: Passing objects via attributes as a JSON string is an anti-pattern. It is slow, brittle (requires parsing), and problematic with encoding special characters.
Properties are designed specifically for passing JavaScript objects and arrays. They are set via a setter, can be typed in TypeScript, and require no serialization.

options.text: element.setAttribute('items-count', items.length) and pass items one by one via attributes
options.explanation: Splitting an array into multiple attributes is extremely inconvenient and inefficient.

options.text: Pass via the data-items data attribute
options.explanation: Data attributes are also string-based — the same problem with JSON.stringify/parse applies.

question: What is the difference between Shadow DOM mode: 'open' and mode: 'closed'?

options.text: open — styles penetrate inside, closed — they do not
options.explanation: mode does not affect style isolation. Both modes encapsulate CSS identically.

options.text: open — shadowRoot is accessible externally via element.shadowRoot, closed — returns null
options.explanation: mode: 'open' allows external JS to obtain a reference via element.shadowRoot. mode: 'closed' returns null — shadowRoot is accessible only within the component's class.

options.text: open — events bubble out, closed — they do not
options.explanation: Event propagation behavior is controlled by the composed parameter, not the Shadow DOM mode.

options.text: open — the component can be used in HTML, closed — only from JS
options.explanation: Both modes allow the component to be used in HTML as well as from JS.

question: You are wrapping a React component in a Custom Element. In which lifecycle method should you call root.unmount()?

options.explanation: In the constructor, the React root has not yet been created — calling unmount is impossible. The constructor is only for attachShadow.
connectedCallback is called when the element is added to the DOM — this is where you call createRoot and render, not unmount.
disconnectedCallback is called when the element is removed from the DOM — this is exactly where resources should be cleaned up: root.unmount(), removeEventListener, clearInterval.
attributeChangedCallback is called when attributes change — this is where you update the render, not call unmount.

question: Which CSS mechanisms can be used to style specific internal parts of a Web Component from outside?

options.explanation: ::part(button) allows styling elements with the attribute part='button' inside the Shadow DOM — this is the intentionally 'open' public styling API.
CSS Custom Properties cross the shadow boundary — the component accepts --my-var and uses it via var(--my-var, default).
Regular selectors do not work inside the Shadow DOM — that is precisely what Shadow DOM is for.
::slotted() allows styling content inserted into component slots — but only direct children, not nested descendants.

question: Content inserted into a slot (<slot>) physically resides in...

options.text: The component's Shadow DOM (moved there by the browser)
options.explanation: The browser does not move the content — this is a common misconception.

options.text: The Light DOM (stays there but is visually rendered in the Shadow DOM)
options.explanation: Slots are a projection, not a move. Content physically stays in the Light DOM (accessible via document.querySelector, page scripts, and global styles) but is visually rendered at the location of the <slot>.

options.text: An isolated tree — accessible from neither Light DOM nor Shadow DOM
options.explanation: No such isolated tree exists — slotted content is accessible via the Light DOM.
The content resides inside the host element in the Light DOM, not directly in body.

question: You are on a team developing the catalog-card Web Component. What elements should be included in the component contract documentation?

options.text: List of attributes with types and default values
options.explanation: Attributes are the public HTML API — their documentation is required for using the component in HTML markup.

options.text: Internal implementation details (how the Shadow DOM is structured inside)
options.explanation: Implementation details should not be documented as part of the contract — they can change. The contract covers only the public API.
CSS Custom Properties are the public styling API. Without documenting them, consumers do not know how to customize the component.
Events are the only feedback mechanism from the component. Their names and payload must be documented for correct subscription.

options.text: Slots with a description of expected content
options.explanation: Slots are the public API for content insertion. Consumers must know which slots exist and what to insert into them.

question: In a micro-frontend project, the Shell (React) listens to events from the Catalog MFE (Web Component). The 'item-selected' event does not reach the Shell. What is the cause?

options.text: React does not support addEventListener for Custom Elements
options.explanation: React works perfectly well with addEventListener on DOM elements. That is not the issue.

options.text: The event was created without composed: true — it gets stuck inside the Shadow DOM
options.explanation: Without composed: true, the event does not cross the shadow boundary. It bubbles up through the Shadow DOM tree but stops at the shadow root and does not reach the document.

options.text: The event name contains a hyphen: 'item-selected'
options.explanation: A hyphen in an event name is perfectly valid and even recommended for namespacing (catalog:item-selected).

options.text: Shell added the listener before Catalog MFE was mounted
options.explanation: The order in which listeners are added only affects already-dispatched events, not the delivery of events across the shadow boundary.
